senses.gloss: Broken into pieces by a blow or a fall.
examples: A *smashed* headlight lay in the middle of the road.
The package arrived with everything inside *smashed*.
He swept up the *smashed* glass before the kids came in.

senses.gloss: Very drunk (informal).
examples: They got totally *smashed* at the wedding.
Half the crew was *smashed* by ten o'clock.

contrast: In American English *smashing* survives mostly in the fixed phrase *a smashing success*; used on its own for "great", it still sounds British.

senses.gloss: Wonderful; very successful.
examples: The fundraiser was a *smashing* success.
Her first show got *smashing* reviews.
They threw a *smashing* party for his retirement.

contrast: Before a noun it is an adjective (*a smiling face*); after *be* it is normally the verb: *She was smiling at me*.

senses.gloss: With a smile on the face.
examples: A *smiling* clerk waved us to the front of the line.
The wall was covered with *smiling* faces.
He gave me a *smiling* nod and kept walking.

senses.gloss: Suddenly and completely in love with someone, or charmed by something.
examples: He was completely *smitten* with his new neighbor.
She's *smitten* — she talks about him all day.
They were *smitten* by the little house the moment they walked in.

senses.gloss: Full of smog — dirty, hazy city air.
examples: It was a hot, *smoggy* afternoon in the valley.
The air downtown is *smoggier* than out by the coast.
We couldn't see the mountains through the *smoggy* haze.

senses.gloss: Full of smoke.
examples: They argued for hours in a *smoke-filled* back room.
Firefighters crawled down the *smoke-filled* hallway.
The deal was made in *smoke-filled* rooms long before the vote.

senses.gloss: Where smoking is not allowed.
examples: The whole campus has been *smoke-free* since 2010.
We booked a *smoke-free* room on the third floor.
City buses and train platforms are *smoke-free*.

senses.gloss: Cured and flavored by hanging in smoke.
examples: We had bagels with *smoked* salmon.
He ordered the *smoked* turkey sandwich.
The store sells *smoked* ham by the pound.

senses.gloss: Made dark, so that you cannot see through it clearly.
examples: The car came with *smoked* windows.
She wore glasses with *smoked* lenses.

senses.gloss: Producing no smoke.
examples: The stove burns *smokeless* fuel.
*Smokeless* tobacco is banned in the stadium.
They switched to a *smokeless* fire pit.

contrast: In *a smoking area* or *the smoking section*, *smoking* is a noun (the activity), not this adjective.

senses.gloss: Giving off smoke.
examples: Firefighters stood in front of the *smoking* ruins.
A *smoking* pan filled the kitchen with a burnt smell.
The email was the *smoking* gun the lawyers needed.

contrast: American spelling is *smoky*, without the *e*.

senses.gloss: Full of smoke, or clouded by it.
examples: The bar was dark and *smoky*.
A *smoky* haze hung over the whole valley.

senses.gloss: Tasting or smelling of smoke.
examples: The cheese has a rich, *smoky* flavor.
This whiskey is *smokier* than the one we tried last time.

contrast: American spelling *smoldering*; British *smouldering*.

senses.gloss: Burning slowly, with smoke but no flame.
examples: Firefighters watered down the *smoldering* debris.
A *smoldering* cigarette had started the whole thing.

senses.gloss: Strong but held in, of a feeling.
examples: There was a *smoldering* resentment between the two brothers.
She gave him a *smoldering* look across the table.

senses.gloss: Flat and even to the touch, with no bumps or lumps.
examples: The stones by the river are worn *smooth*.
Beat the sauce until it's completely *smooth*.
She ran her hand over the *smooth* tabletop.

senses.gloss: Going along without jolts or problems.
examples: We had a *smooth* flight to Denver.
The move to the new system was *smoother* than anyone expected.

senses.gloss: Charming and confident in a way you do not quite trust, of a person.
examples: He's a *smooth* talker — don't sign anything today.
The salesman was a little too *smooth* for my taste.

senses.gloss: So heavy or so constant that you feel you cannot breathe.
examples: The *smothering* heat made it hard to sleep.
She moved out to get away from her mother's *smothering* attention.
A *smothering* blanket of smoke settled over the town.

senses.gloss: Too pleased with yourself, in a way that annoys other people.
examples: He had a *smug* look on his face after the test.
Nobody likes a *smug* winner.
She got *smugger* with every point she scored.

senses.gloss: Brought into or out of a country secretly and illegally.
examples: Police found *smuggled* cigarettes in the back of the truck.
The museum returned several *smuggled* artifacts.
*Smuggled* goods are seized at the border every day.

contrast: *Make it snappy* means "hurry up".

senses.gloss: Quick, short and lively.
examples: The movie has *snappy* dialogue and a short runtime.
Give me a *snappier* headline for the front page.

senses.gloss: Stylish and sharp-looking (informal).
examples: He showed up in a *snappy* blue suit.
That's a *snappy* pair of shoes.

senses.gloss: Stylish and eye-catching, often a little flashy (informal).
examples: He drove up in a *snazzy* red convertible.
That's a *snazzy* jacket — is it new?
Their new website looks *snazzier* than ours.

contrast: *sneak* is also a noun and a verb; as an adjective it lives only in fixed pairs — *a sneak attack*, *a sneak preview*, *a sneak peek*.

senses.gloss: Done without warning, before anyone can react.
examples: It was a *sneak* attack on a sleeping base.
The studio held a *sneak* preview on Thursday night.
She gave us a *sneak* peek at the new design.

contrast: Almost always with *suspicion*, *feeling* or *admiration*: a quiet thought you do not say out loud.

senses.gloss: Felt quietly and kept to yourself.
examples: I have a *sneaking* suspicion that he already knows.
She had a *sneaking* admiration for her rival.
There was a *sneaking* feeling that the deal was too good.

senses.gloss: Acting in secret to get what you want, in a way people find dishonest.
examples: That was a *sneaky* way to get out of paying.
He's *sneakier* than his brother ever was.
Don't be *sneaky* about it — just ask her.

senses.gloss: Insulting in an indirect, sly way.
examples: He made a *snide* remark about her accent.
The review was full of *snide* comments.
Her tone was *snide* rather than funny.

senses.gloss: Looking down on people you think have less money, taste or education.
examples: The staff was polite but a little *snobbish*.
He has a *snobbish* attitude about wine.
Don't be *snobbish* about where other people shop.

contrast: *snobby* is the casual spoken word; *snobbish* is the one you write.

senses.gloss: Acting superior to other people (informal).
examples: The restaurant felt *snobby* the minute we walked in.
Her new friends are *snobbier* than she is.
He's not *snobby* about music at all.

ru: любопытный, сующий нос в чужие дела

senses.gloss: Too interested in other people's private business (informal).
examples: Our *snoopy* neighbor watches every car on the street.
Don't be *snoopy* about other people's mail.
She got *snoopier* after she retired.

senses.gloss: Treating other people as beneath you (informal).
examples: The hostess gave us a *snooty* look.
It's a *snooty* little shop on the corner.
The service got *snootier* the longer we waited.

contrast: Rude and dismissive — fine in speech between friends, never in writing about a real person.

senses.gloss: Young and annoyingly sure of himself (informal, insulting).
examples: Some *snot-nosed* kid told me I was parked wrong.
He was a *snot-nosed* rookie back then.
I'm not taking orders from a *snot-nosed* intern.

senses.gloss: Rude and superior (informal).
examples: Don't get *snotty* with me.
She sent a *snotty* email to the whole team.
His tone got *snottier* with every question.

senses.gloss: Covered with mucus from the nose.
examples: Wipe that *snotty* nose before we go in.
The toddler handed me a *snotty* tissue.

senses.gloss: With snow on top, of a mountain.
examples: *Snow-capped* peaks rose behind the town.
We could see the *snow-capped* mountains from the hotel.
The postcard showed a *snow-capped* volcano.

senses.gloss: With snow lying all over it.
examples: We drove slowly down the *snow-covered* road.
The *snow-covered* fields went on for miles.
By morning every car on the block was *snow-covered*.

form: compound — noun + adjective, "as white as snow"

senses.gloss: Pure white.
examples: He had a *snow-white* beard.
The tablecloth was *snow-white*.
She wore a *snow-white* dress to the ceremony.

senses.gloss: Unable to travel or get out because of heavy snow.
examples: We were *snowbound* at the cabin for three days.
A *snowbound* village waited all week for the plows.
The storm left hundreds of travelers *snowbound* at the airport.

senses.gloss: With a lot of snow.
examples: It was a cold, *snowy* January.
This is the *snowiest* winter in twenty years.

senses.gloss: White like snow.
examples: He stroked his *snowy* beard.
*Snowy* sheets hung on the line behind the house.

senses.gloss: With a short nose that turns up at the end.
examples: A *snub-nosed* boy answered the door.
She has her father's *snub-nosed* face.

senses.gloss: With a very short barrel, of a gun.
examples: He carried a *snub-nosed* revolver.
The detective's *snub-nosed* .38 lay on the desk.

senses.gloss: Warm, small and comfortable.
examples: The cabin was tiny but *snug*.
The kids were *snug* under two blankets.

senses.gloss: Fitting closely, sometimes a little too closely.
examples: The jacket is a little *snug* across the shoulders.
These boots feel *snugger* than the last pair.

contrast: Also used as an adverb (*He plays so-so*), and always written with a hyphen.

senses.gloss: Neither good nor bad; average (informal).
examples: The food was *so-so*, but the view was great.
He got *so-so* grades his first semester.
How was the movie? *So-so*.

senses.gloss: Full of soap, or covered with it.
examples: Wash the pan in hot *soapy* water.
The floor was still *soapy* and slippery.
This water is *soapier* than it needs to be.

senses.gloss: Rising fast, of prices or numbers.
examples: *Soaring* rents have pushed families out of the city.
The airline blamed *soaring* fuel costs.

senses.gloss: Rising very high into the air.
examples: The church has a *soaring* ceiling.
She held the *soaring* high note at the end of the song.

senses.gloss: Not drunk.
examples: He's been *sober* for six years.
Someone has to stay *sober* and drive.
She was perfectly *sober* when she said it.

senses.gloss: Serious and unexcited.
examples: It was a *sober* assessment of the damage.
The mood in the room was *sober*.

contrast: *sobering* is the thing that makes you think; a person who is not drunk is *sober*.

senses.gloss: Making you suddenly serious about how bad something is.
examples: The accident report makes for *sobering* reading.
It was a *sobering* reminder of how fast things change.
The numbers in the study are *sobering*.

contrast: *sociable* describes a person who enjoys company; *social* describes society or gatherings (*a social event*). You cannot say "a sociable problem".

senses.gloss: Enjoying the company of other people.
examples: She's a *sociable* kid who makes friends anywhere.
He's not very *sociable* before his first coffee.
The dogs are *sociable* with strangers.

position: attributive only — except the informal *He's very social* (= sociable)
contrast: *social* is about society or about gatherings; a friendly person is *sociable*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with society and how people live together.
examples: The city is facing serious *social* problems.
She studies *social* change in small towns.

senses.gloss: Having to do with spending time with other people.
examples: We met at a *social* event at the club.
He has a busy *social* life.

contrast: Also a noun: *She is a socialist*.

senses.gloss: Based on socialism — the idea that the state or the workers should own the main industries.
examples: The party ran on a *socialist* platform.
He studies *socialist* movements in postwar Europe.
*Socialist* governments came to power across the region.

contrast: American spelling *-ized*; British *-ised*.

senses.gloss: Run and paid for by the government instead of private companies.
examples: Critics call the plan *socialized* medicine.
He argued against *socialized* health care for an hour.

senses.gloss: Trained to behave well with others.
examples: The puppy is well *socialized* around children.
Kids who are poorly *socialized* struggle in big groups.

contrast: *societal* is formal and means "of society as a whole"; everyday English says *social*.

senses.gloss: Belonging to society as a whole.
examples: The report looks at the *societal* costs of long commutes.
*Societal* attitudes toward the issue have changed fast.
These are *societal* problems, not personal failings.

senses.gloss: Having to do with both society and culture.
examples: The study takes a *sociocultural* approach to language learning.
*Sociocultural* factors shape what people eat.
They mapped the *sociocultural* history of the neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Having to do with both money and social position.
examples: Test scores track *socioeconomic* status closely.
The two neighborhoods differ in *socioeconomic* background.
The researchers controlled for *socioeconomic* factors.

senses.gloss: Having to do with the study of society.
examples: She published a *sociological* study of small-town churches.
From a *sociological* point of view, the change is enormous.
He teaches *sociological* theory to first-year students.

senses.gloss: Behaving with no conscience and no feeling for other people.
examples: The novel's villain is charming and *sociopathic*.
Experts described the behavior as *sociopathic*.
He shows *sociopathic* traits under pressure.

senses.gloss: Teaching by asking question after question, in the manner of Socrates.
examples: Law schools still teach by the *Socratic* method.
The class was run as a *Socratic* dialogue.
He answered every question with another one, in true *Socratic* style.

senses.gloss: Soaked through with water, and heavy because of it.
examples: We walked the last mile in *sodden* shoes.
The field was *sodden* after three days of rain.
He pulled off his *sodden* coat and hung it by the door.

takes: *on* + noun in the sense "not strict": *soft on crime*

senses.gloss: Easy to press or bend; not hard.
examples: The mattress is too *soft* for my back.
Leave the butter out until it's *soft*.

senses.gloss: Smooth and pleasant to touch.
examples: That blanket is the *softest* thing she owns.
The baby has *soft* pink skin.

senses.gloss: Quiet; not loud.
examples: She answered in a *soft* voice.
The music was *soft* enough to talk over.

senses.gloss: Gentle; not strict enough.
examples: The judge is *soft* on first offenders.
Don't be too *soft* with them or nothing gets done.

senses.gloss: Boiled only a few minutes, so the yolk is still runny.
examples: He had a *soft-boiled* egg and toast.
I like my eggs *soft-boiled*.
The diner serves *soft-boiled* eggs all day.

senses.gloss: Speaking in a quiet, gentle voice.
senses.ru: с тихим голосом, мягкий в разговоре
examples: He's a *soft-spoken* man who never interrupts.
She was *soft-spoken* but completely firm.
Our *soft-spoken* coach has never yelled at anyone.

senses.gloss: Wet and limp, in a way that spoils food or ground.
examples: Nobody wants *soggy* fries.
The cereal went *soggy* in the milk.
The bottom of the pie was even *soggier* the next day.

contrast: *soiled* is the polite, slightly formal word for dirty — hospitals and hotels say *soiled linens*, not "dirty sheets".

senses.gloss: Made dirty by use.
examples: Put the *soiled* towels in the blue bin.
The nurse changed the *soiled* sheets.
His shirt was *soiled* at the collar.

contrast: *solar* means "of the sun" as a scientific term; a bright day is *sunny*, never "solar".

senses.gloss: Of or from the sun.
examples: A *solar* eclipse will be visible from the coast.
There are eight planets in the *solar* system.

senses.gloss: Using the sun's energy.
examples: They put *solar* panels on the roof last spring.
The whole house runs on *solar* power.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (*a sold-out show*), two separate words after the verb (*The show sold out in an hour*).

senses.gloss: With every ticket already sold.
examples: They played to a *sold-out* arena.
The concert has been *sold-out* for weeks.
It's a *sold-out* crowd tonight.

senses.gloss: Very serious, with no smiling.
examples: The room went *solemn* when he stood up to speak.
She had a *solemn* look on her face all morning.

senses.gloss: Formal and binding.
examples: He made a *solemn* promise to pay it back.
The new officers took a *solemn* oath.

senses.gloss: Showing careful, almost anxious concern for someone.
examples: The host was *solicitous* about our comfort all evening.
She is *solicitous* of her elderly father.
A *solicitous* waiter refilled every glass before it was empty.

contrast: *three solid hours* means "three hours without a break" — a fourth, time meaning.

senses.gloss: Hard and keeping its shape; not liquid or gas.
examples: The lake was frozen *solid* by January.
Water becomes *solid* at 32 degrees.

senses.gloss: Strongly built and not likely to break.
examples: It's an old table, but it's *solid*.
They built a *solid* stone wall around the yard.

senses.gloss: Made of one material all the way through.
examples: The ring is *solid* gold.
The door is *solid* wood, not veneer.

senses.gloss: Dependable and good, without being brilliant.
examples: He gave a *solid* performance in the second half.
The case rests on *solid* evidence.

contrast: American spelling *-colored*; British *-coloured*.

senses.gloss: All one color, with no pattern.
examples: Wear a *solid-colored* shirt for the photo.
She prefers *solid-colored* dresses to prints.
The uniform has to be *solid-colored*.

senses.gloss: Built from solid electronic parts, with nothing moving inside.
examples: The laptop has a *solid-state* drive.
*Solid-state* amplifiers replaced the old tube ones.
It's a *solid-state* sensor with no moving parts.

position: both — the "only one" sense goes before a noun
contrast: *solitary* means alone by habit or by choice; *lonely* means sad because you are alone. Russian одинокий covers both.

senses.gloss: Alone, or done alone.
examples: He took a *solitary* walk along the beach.
Tigers are *solitary* animals.

senses.gloss: Only one, and no more.
examples: Not a *solitary* word was said about the money.
A *solitary* streetlight lit the whole block.

contrast: Also an adverb (*She flew solo*) and a noun (*a piano solo*).

senses.gloss: Done by one person alone.
examples: She released her first *solo* album in March.
He made a *solo* flight across the Atlantic.
The climb was *solo*, with no support team.

senses.gloss: Able to dissolve in a liquid.
examples: Salt is *soluble* in water.
The tablets come in a *soluble* form.
Vitamin D is fat-*soluble*, so take it with a meal.

senses.gloss: Able to be solved.
examples: The puzzle is *solvable* in under a minute.
These are *solvable* problems if we start now.
He treats every crisis as *solvable*.

contrast: Also a noun: *a solvent* is a liquid that dissolves other things.

senses.gloss: Having enough money to pay what you owe.
examples: The company is barely *solvent*.
Two good quarters kept the firm *solvent*.
A bank has to stay *solvent* to keep its license.

contrast: Also a noun — *a Somali* (a person) and *Somali* (the language). The country is *Somalia*.

senses.gloss: From Somalia, or having to do with Somalia and its people.
examples: She grew up in a *Somali* neighborhood in Minneapolis.
The restaurant serves *Somali* food.
Many of the students in the class are *Somali*.

contrast: American spelling *somber*; British *sombre*.

senses.gloss: Sad and serious in mood.
examples: The mood at the meeting was *somber*.
She read the news in a *somber* voice.

senses.gloss: Dark and dull in color.
examples: He wore a *somber* gray suit to the service.
The room is painted in *somber* browns.

senses.gloss: Having to do with sound or the speed of sound.
examples: The jet made a *sonic* boom over the coast.
The band is known for its *sonic* experiments.
Engineers measured the *sonic* range of the hall.

senses.gloss: Deep, full and pleasant in sound.
examples: He has a deep, *sonorous* voice.
The bells were *sonorous* in the empty square.
She read the poem in *sonorous* tones.

senses.gloss: Making pain or worry easier to bear.
examples: Her voice on the phone was *soothing*.
He put on some *soothing* music and lay down.
The cream is *soothing* on a sunburn.

senses.gloss: Covered or blackened with soot.
examples: He wiped his *sooty* hands on a rag.
The wall above the stove was *sooty*.
The chimney got *sootier* every winter.

contrast: Also a noun — *a sophomore* is a second-year student. As an adjective it means "second in a series": *a sophomore album*.

senses.gloss: Of the second year of high school or college, or second in a series.
examples: She's taking chemistry her *sophomore* year.
The band's *sophomore* album flopped.
He had a *sophomore* slump after a great rookie season.

senses.gloss: Making you sleepy.
examples: The lecture had a *soporific* effect on the whole class.
He read the list in a *soporific* monotone.
The heat in that room is *soporific*.

senses.gloss: Morally dirty — involving lies, greed or shabby behavior.
examples: The paper printed every *sordid* detail.
It's a *sordid* story of money and lies.
The whole business was more *sordid* than anyone expected.

contrast: *a sore point* is a subject that upsets someone. Do not confuse *sore* (hurting) with *sorry*.

senses.gloss: Painful, especially from use or infection.
examples: I woke up with a *sore* throat.
My legs were *sorer* the day after the hike.
Her shoulder is still *sore* from the fall.

senses.gloss: Annoyed and hurt about something (informal).
examples: He's still *sore* about losing the bet.
Don't be a *sore* loser.

contrast: *sorrowful* is literary; everyday American English says *sad*.

senses.gloss: Full of deep sadness, or showing it.
examples: She gave me a *sorrowful* look and said nothing.
The song is slow and *sorrowful*.
His face was *sorrowful* but calm.

senses.gloss: Wanted by many people, and therefore hard to get.
examples: He's the *most sought-after* photographer in town.
These tickets are highly *sought-after*.
It's a *sought-after* address on the north side.

senses.gloss: Full of deep feeling that you can hear or see.
examples: She sang a *soulful* version of the old hymn.
The dog gave him a *soulful* look.
His playing is *soulful* and unhurried.

senses.gloss: With no warmth or feeling in it.
examples: They tore down the old theater and put up a *soulless* office block.
The remake is technically perfect and completely *soulless*.
It's *soulless* work, but it pays the rent.

contrast: Also a noun (*a loud sound*) and a verb (*That sounds good*). *safe and sound* is a fixed phrase.

senses.gloss: In good condition; not damaged or ill.
examples: The inspector said the roof is *sound*.
The kids came back safe and *sound*.

senses.gloss: Sensible and based on good reasoning.
examples: That's *sound* advice.
His plan is *sounder* than mine.

senses.gloss: Deep and unbroken, of sleep.
examples: She's a *sound* sleeper — the storm never woke her.
He fell into a *sound* sleep on the couch.

form: fixed phrase — *sound* here is an old adverb meaning "deeply"
contrast: Only after a verb. Never "a sound asleep baby" — before a noun use *a sleeping baby*.

senses.gloss: Deeply asleep and hard to wake.
examples: The baby was *sound asleep* by seven.
Both kids were *sound asleep* in the back seat.
He's *sound asleep* — don't wake him up.

senses.gloss: Built so that sound cannot pass through.
examples: The studio is completely *soundproof*.
They put in *soundproof* windows facing the highway.
It's not a *soundproof* room, so keep your voice down.

senses.gloss: Too thin and watery, of food.
examples: The risotto came out *soupy*.
Add more rice if it still looks *soupy*.

senses.gloss: Thick and heavy, of fog or air.
examples: We drove through *soupy* fog all morning.
The August air was *soupier* than ever.

contrast: *go sour* is also used of plans and relationships: *The deal went sour*.

senses.gloss: Sharp in taste, like a lemon.
examples: These cherries are too *sour* to eat raw.
She likes *sour* candy.

senses.gloss: Spoiled, of milk or cream.
examples: The milk has gone *sour*.
There was a *sour* smell in the fridge.

senses.gloss: Unfriendly and bad-tempered.
examples: He gave me a *sour* look.
Her mood got *sourer* as the day went on.

senses.gloss: Turned unfriendly or bitter, of a relationship or mood.
examples: *Soured* relations between the two countries dragged on for years.
He left the company and a *soured* friendship behind him.

senses.gloss: Turned sour, of milk or cream.
examples: A carton of *soured* milk sat on the counter.
You can still bake with slightly *soured* milk.

contrast: Also a noun (*the South*) and an adverb (*drive south*). For a region or its people use *southern*: *southern cooking*, not "south cooking".

senses.gloss: On or facing the south side.
examples: Their office is on the *south* side of the building.
A *south* wind brought warmer air.
We parked by the *south* entrance.

contrast: Also a noun (*a South African*). Both words are capitalized, with no hyphen.

senses.gloss: From South Africa, or having to do with it.
examples: He's a *South African* journalist based in London.
We tried a *South African* wine with dinner.
Two of the players are *South African*.

contrast: Also a noun (*a South American*).

senses.gloss: From South America, or having to do with it.
examples: The bird is native to *South American* rainforests.
She writes about *South American* politics.
Most of the group is *South American*.

contrast: Also a noun (*a South Korean*).

senses.gloss: From South Korea, or having to do with it.
examples: The company is *South Korean*.
He drives a *South Korean* car.
*South Korean* films have won major prizes.

senses.gloss: Traveling toward the south.
examples: The *southbound* lanes are closed until noon.
We took the *southbound* train from Penn Station.
Most of the traffic this morning is *southbound*.

contrast: Also a noun and an adverb. For a whole region the usual adjective is *southeastern*.

senses.gloss: In or facing the southeast.
examples: The storm hit the *southeast* corner of the state.
A *southeast* wind is pushing the smoke inland.
Their farm is in *southeast* Kansas.

senses.gloss: In or from the southeast part of a country or region.
examples: She grew up in *southeastern* Ohio.
The plant grows across the *southeastern* United States.
*Southeastern* Europe was hit hardest by the drought.

contrast: An *-ly* word that is an adjective, not an adverb. A *southerly* wind blows from the south, but a *southerly* course goes toward the south.

senses.gloss: From the south, or toward the south.
senses.ru: южный, идущий с юга или на юг
examples: A *southerly* wind kept the night warm.
We took a *more southerly* route to avoid the snow.
The island is the *most southerly* point of the country.

comparison: not gradable — it is already a superlative

senses.gloss: Farthest to the south.
examples: Key West is the *southernmost* city in the continental United States.
They reached the *southernmost* tip of the island at dusk.
This is the *southernmost* vineyard in the state.

contrast: Also a noun and an adverb. For a whole region the usual adjective is *southwestern*.

senses.gloss: In or facing the southwest.
examples: A *southwest* wind carried the smoke into town.
The house has a *southwest* exposure and gets sun all afternoon.
They drove through *southwest* Texas for two days.

senses.gloss: In or from the southwest part of a country or region.
examples: *Southwestern* cooking uses a lot of chiles.
The rain never reached the *southwestern* counties.
He moved to a small *southwestern* town for the dry air.

contrast: Also a noun — *the sovereign* is a king or queen.

senses.gloss: Independent and governing itself, of a country.
examples: Ukraine is a *sovereign* state.
They demanded *sovereign* control of their own waters.

senses.gloss: Holding the highest power.
examples: In a monarchy the king is *sovereign*.
Congress holds *sovereign* authority over the budget.
